newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - US refining margins improve but may not last.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - US refining margins improve but may not last.

text.p: A recent recovery in margins is good news for U.S. oil refiners who suffered a sharp decrease in the third quarter and through October, though some analysts expect that improvement will not be sustainable.

Refiners' margins have improved sharply over the last few weeks in the Gulf Coast, East Coast and Midwest, though not on the West Coast, as crude oil weakened while gasoline lagged those losses and distillates -- heating oil and diesel -- remained relatively strong.

The market has seen "really good demand numbers on the gasoline and distillates. That, in combination with the dip in crude prices has boosted margins," said Tom Knight, trader with Fina Inc in New Jersey. "With demand staying very strong, refiners are a little happier," Knight added.

The demand growth has been seen mainly in distillates. According to the latest Energy Information Administration (EIA) report, U.S. distillate fuel demand totalled 3.590 million barrels per day (bpd) last week, up 13.3 percent year-on-year. Gasoline demand was at 7.889 million bpd, an increase of 0.8 percent from 1995.
But the boost in margins has led refineries to maximize their output, helping to boost the low inventories, particularly in heating oil.
"Heating oil seems to be coming into its seasonal balance," said Alan Struth, chief economist with Phillips Petroleum.
Distillate production was still near record-high levels last week at 3.598 million bpd, according to the latest American Petroleum Institute weekly report.

The year-on-year deficit in distillate stocks continued to narrow and was at about 15 million barrels in the latest API report from more than 21 million barrels in early September. Much of the increase was in the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.

And as the inventories increase, margins are likely to head lower. "Refineries clearly shifted to make as much heating oil as they could, but there's sufficient capacity in the system to meet the demand for heating oil and gosoline," Struth said.

"We could see more production if they think its necessary," said Frank Knuettel, analyst with Prudential Bache Securities. The inventory situation "has been hyped-up the whole year," he added, and the low stocks are not a serious problem.
Also, the backwardation in the products markets, with nearby prices at a premium to supplies for later delivery, will also push refineries to keep operations at relatively high levels, traders said.
"There's still ample incentive for refineries to keep production high," said Knight.
A number of refineries have brought or are shortly due to bring back on line units which were down for seasonal maintenance, another reason to worry that margins may again weaken.
